questions.stem: Which carbohydrate is a polysaccharide that forms the cell walls of plants?
options: Sucrose
Peptidoglycan
Cellulose
Glycogen
questions.explanation: Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide made of glucose units; it gives plant cell walls their strength. Glycogen is an energy-storage polysaccharide in animals and sucrose is a disaccharide. Peptidoglycan forms bacterial, not plant, cell walls.

questions.stem: How is energy stored as carbohydrate in animals and in plants?
options: As starch in animals and as glycogen in plants
As cellulose in animals and as starch in plants
As glycogen in animals and as cellulose in plants
As glycogen in animals and as starch in plants
questions.explanation: Animals store glucose as glycogen, mainly in the liver and muscles. Plants store it as starch. Cellulose is structural, and animals do not make it.

questions.stem: What are the building blocks of proteins, and which bond joins them?
options: Monosaccharides, joined by peptide bonds
Amino acids, joined by glycosidic bonds
Fatty acids, joined by ester bonds
Amino acids, joined by peptide bonds
questions.explanation: Proteins are chains of amino acids linked by peptide bonds formed in condensation reactions. Glycosidic bonds join monosaccharides, and ester bonds join fatty acids to glycerol.

questions.stem: Why does a change to a single amino acid in a protein sometimes stop the protein working?
options: It turns the protein into a lipid, which cannot dissolve in the cytoplasm
It doubles the length of the chain, so the protein no longer fits in the cell
It can change how the chain folds, altering the protein's three-dimensional shape
It removes all of the peptide bonds, so the chain breaks into separate amino acids
questions.explanation: The sequence of amino acids (primary structure) determines how the chain folds into its final shape, and a protein's function depends on that shape. A different amino acid can change the bonds that hold the fold, as with an enzyme's active site.

questions.stem: A triglyceride is made of:
options: three glycerols and one fatty acid
one glucose and three fatty acids
one glycerol and three amino acids
one glycerol and three fatty acids
questions.explanation: A triglyceride forms when three fatty acids are joined to one glycerol by ester bonds. Triglycerides are the main lipids used for long-term energy storage and insulation.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares lipids and carbohydrates as energy stores?
options: Lipids release about twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates
Carbohydrates release about twice as much energy per gram as lipids
Lipids and carbohydrates release the same energy per gram
Lipids store energy only in plants, and carbohydrates only in animals
questions.explanation: Fats release roughly 37 kJ per gram when respired, compared with roughly 17 kJ per gram for carbohydrates, so they are compact long-term stores. Carbohydrates are used for faster, short-term release.

questions.stem: Which lipid is the main structural component of cell membranes?
options: Phospholipid
Triglyceride
Wax
Cellulose
questions.explanation: A phospholipid has a hydrophilic phosphate head and two hydrophobic fatty acid tails, so it forms bilayers in water. Triglycerides are energy stores, and cellulose is a carbohydrate.

questions.stem: Which enzyme begins the chemical digestion of starch in the mouth?
options: Amylase
Lipase
Protease
Maltase
questions.explanation: Salivary amylase breaks starch into maltose, a disaccharide. Pancreatic amylase continues this in the small intestine. Lipase digests lipids and protease digests proteins.

questions.stem: What are the products of the complete digestion of a triglyceride by lipase?
options: Amino acids and glycerol
Glucose and fatty acids
Maltose and glycerol
Fatty acids and glycerol
questions.explanation: Lipase hydrolyses the ester bonds of a triglyceride, releasing fatty acids and glycerol. These are absorbed by the villi of the small intestine.

questions.stem: Which row correctly matches a digestive enzyme with its substrate and product?
options: Protease: proteins to polypeptides and amino acids
Amylase: proteins to polypeptides and amino acids
Lipase: starch to maltose and glucose
Protease: lipids to fatty acids and glycerol
questions.explanation: Proteases such as pepsin and trypsin break peptide bonds, producing shorter polypeptides and then amino acids. Amylase acts on starch, and lipase acts on lipids.

questions.stem: Bile contains no enzymes, yet removing the gall bladder can reduce how quickly fats are digested after a fatty meal. Why?
options: Bile lowers the pH of the small intestine to the optimum pH for lipase activity
Bile breaks fats into fatty acids, which lipase then converts into glycerol
Bile emulsifies fats into small droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase
Bile contains lipase in an inactive form, which is released only from the gall bladder
questions.explanation: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. Its bile salts break large fat globules into small droplets (emulsification). This is physical, not chemical, digestion, and it gives lipase a much larger surface to act on. Bile is alkaline, so it raises rather than lowers the pH.

questions.stem: How do the villi of the small intestine increase the rate of nutrient absorption?
options: They store nutrients until the blood sugar level falls
They greatly increase the surface area available for absorption
They secrete amylase, lipase and protease into the gut
They slow the passage of food by contracting rhythmically
questions.explanation: Villi are finger-like folds, and the epithelial cells covering them have microvilli, together giving an enormous surface area. Secreting digestive enzymes is mainly the role of the pancreas and glands, not the villi.

questions.stem: Which feature of a villus helps maintain a steep concentration gradient for glucose absorption?
options: A large central lacteal that stores glucose for later use
A dense network of capillaries that carries absorbed glucose away
A thick layer of smooth muscle that pushes glucose back into the gut
A waxy cuticle that stops glucose escaping from the villus
questions.explanation: Blood flowing through the capillaries constantly removes absorbed glucose, keeping its concentration in the villus lower than in the gut. Lacteals are lymph vessels that absorb the products of fat digestion, not stores of glucose.

questions.stem: Fatty acids and glycerol, after absorption, are reassembled into lipids in the epithelial cells of the villus. Into which structure do these lipids mainly pass?
options: The lacteal, a lymph vessel in the villus
The capillary network, as free glucose
The hepatic portal vein, as amino acids
The microvilli, where they are stored
questions.explanation: Lipids are packaged and pass into the lacteal, which drains into the lymphatic system and eventually into the blood. Glucose and amino acids, by contrast, enter the capillaries and travel to the liver.

questions.stem: Why are capillary walls well suited to exchanging materials with body cells?
options: They are thick and muscular, so they can pump materials out to cells
They contain valves that push materials into the tissues
They are lined with villi that increase their surface area
They are only one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance
questions.explanation: Capillary walls are a single layer of flattened endothelial cells, so substances diffuse a very short distance. Capillaries are also very numerous and narrow, giving a large surface area and slow blood flow. Valves are found in veins.

questions.stem: In a closed circulatory system, which statement is correct?
options: Blood carries no oxygen because cells exchange gases directly with air
Blood stays within vessels and is pumped at high pressure to all tissues
Blood leaves the vessels and bathes the organs directly in a body cavity
Blood flows slowly at low pressure because there is no heart
questions.explanation: In a closed system, as in mammals, blood is always contained in the heart and vessels. This lets it travel at high pressure and speed and be directed to the tissues that need it. In an open system, as in insects, the fluid bathes the organs directly.

questions.stem: Mammals have a double circulation, in which blood passes through the heart twice in each complete circuit. What is the main advantage?
options: Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix fully, so every tissue gets the same blood
Blood pressure in the lungs is raised to match that in the rest of the body
Blood returning from the lungs can be repumped at high pressure to the body
Blood can be oxygenated twice, once in the lungs and once in the heart
questions.explanation: Pressure falls as blood passes through the lung capillaries. Returning it to the left ventricle lets it be pumped at high pressure to the body. Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are kept separate, not mixed, and the lung circuit is kept at lower pressure to protect the delicate capillaries.

questions.stem: In which part of the nephron does filtration of the blood take place?
options: The distal tubule and collecting duct
The glomerulus and Bowman's capsule
The loop of Henle
The collecting duct
questions.explanation: Blood pressure forces water and small solutes out of the glomerulus, a knot of capillaries, into Bowman's capsule. This forms the filtrate. Later sections of the nephron modify the filtrate by reabsorption and secretion.

questions.stem: Which part of the nephron reabsorbs most of the filtered glucose, amino acids, water and sodium ions?
options: Loop of Henle
Proximal tubule
Collecting duct
Bowman's capsule
questions.explanation: The proximal tubule reabsorbs all of the glucose and amino acids, plus most of the water and sodium, back into the blood. Its cells have microvilli and many mitochondria for active transport.

questions.stem: Which substance is normally absent from the glomerular filtrate of a healthy person?
options: Sodium ions
Plasma proteins
Glucose
Urea
questions.explanation: Plasma proteins and blood cells are too large to pass through the filtration barrier, so they stay in the blood. Glucose, urea, ions and water are small and are all filtered.

questions.stem: The table shows concentrations (g per 100 mL) in a healthy person. Plasma: protein 8.0, glucose 0.10, urea 0.03. Filtrate: protein 0, glucose 0.10, urea 0.03. Urine: protein 0, glucose 0, urea 2.0. What explains the urea result?
options: Urea is made in the loop of Henle from the glucose that is removed
Urea is reabsorbed faster than water, so its concentration rises
Most of the water in the filtrate is reabsorbed, concentrating the urea
Urea is too large to be filtered, so it is added later by secretion only
questions.explanation: Urea is filtered at the same concentration as in plasma, but most of the filtrate's water is reabsorbed along the tubule and collecting duct. The urea left behind becomes about 67 times more concentrated. Urea is made in the liver, not the kidney.

questions.stem: Glucose appears in the urine of a person with untreated diabetes, even though their nephrons are undamaged. What is the best explanation?
options: The filtered glucose exceeds the amount the carrier proteins can reabsorb
The glomerulus filters glucose only when the blood sugar level is high
The collecting duct secretes extra glucose into the urine when it is high
The loop of Henle converts urea into glucose when insulin is absent
questions.explanation: Glucose is always filtered. Normally carrier proteins in the proximal tubule reabsorb all of it, but they can work only so fast. When blood glucose is very high, the filtered load exceeds this maximum and the excess stays in the urine. This is why urine tests help diagnose diabetes.

questions.stem: What is meant by tubular secretion in the nephron?
options: Filtration of small molecules from the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule under pressure
Release of hormones from the nephron into the blood to control urine volume
Active transport of substances such as H⁺ and some drugs from blood into the tubule
Passive movement of water from the tubule back into the surrounding capillaries
questions.explanation: Secretion moves substances from the capillaries into the tubule, mainly in the proximal and distal tubules. It removes wastes and excess ions such as H⁺ and K⁺ that were not filtered, and it helps regulate blood pH.

questions.stem: What is the main role of the collecting duct?
options: Reabsorbing all the glucose and amino acids from the filtrate
Secreting plasma proteins into the urine to remove excess protein
Reabsorbing a variable amount of water, which sets the final urine concentration
Filtering blood plasma under high pressure to form the first filtrate in the nephron
questions.explanation: Water leaves the collecting duct into the salty tissue of the medulla. How much leaves depends on the body's water balance, so the duct sets how concentrated the final urine is. Glucose and amino acids are fully reabsorbed earlier, in the proximal tubule.

questions.stem: A urine test shows a large amount of protein in a patient's urine. Which part of the nephron is most likely to be damaged?
options: The distal tubule, failing to secrete hydrogen ions into the urine
The glomerulus, letting large molecules pass into the filtrate
The collecting duct, failing to reabsorb water from the urine
The loop of Henle, failing to create a salt gradient in the medulla
questions.explanation: Proteins are normally too large to cross the glomerular filter, so protein in urine suggests the filter is damaged. Problems with water reabsorption would change urine volume and concentration, not let proteins through.

questions.stem: Enzymes speed up metabolic reactions by:
options: supplying ATP to the substrate
lowering the activation energy of the reaction
raising the temperature of the cell
increasing the energy released by the reaction
questions.explanation: Enzymes are biological catalysts. They provide an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more substrate molecules can react at body temperature. They do not change the overall energy released.

questions.stem: The active site of an enzyme is:
options: the part of the enzyme that is used up and lost when the product forms
the region that is identical in shape for all enzymes in a cell
the region where the substrate binds, with a shape complementary to it
the region that binds ATP to supply energy for every reaction
questions.explanation: The active site is a small region whose shape and chemistry are complementary to the substrate, which is why enzymes are specific. Enzymes are not used up and can be reused many times.

questions.stem: How does the induced-fit model of enzyme action differ from the lock-and-key model?
options: The active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds, rather than being rigid
The substrate changes shape to fit a rigid active site, rather than the enzyme changing
The enzyme binds any substrate, rather than one with a complementary shape
The active site forms only after the product is released, rather than before binding
questions.explanation: In the lock-and-key model the active site is a rigid, exact fit. In the induced-fit model the active site is flexible and moulds around the substrate as it binds, which strains the substrate's bonds. The induced-fit model better explains how enzymes lower activation energy.

questions.stem: Why does each enzyme usually catalyse only one reaction?
options: Only one substrate has a shape complementary to its active site
Each enzyme is destroyed after it catalyses one reaction
Each enzyme is found in only one organelle of the cell
Only one reaction in a cell needs a lower activation energy
questions.explanation: Specificity comes from the shape and chemistry of the active site, which match only a particular substrate. Enzymes are reused many times, and many are found in several places in the cell.

questions.stem: Why does the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction fall sharply above the enzyme's optimum temperature?
options: Bonds holding the enzyme's shape break, so the active site loses its shape
The substrate molecules move too slowly to collide with the active site
The enzyme is used up faster as more product forms at high temperature
The products block the active site because they form too quickly
questions.explanation: High temperatures break the hydrogen and other bonds that maintain the enzyme's tertiary structure. The active site changes shape and no longer fits the substrate: the enzyme is denatured. Molecules move faster, not slower, as temperature rises.

questions.stem: An enzyme kept at 5 °C shows little activity, but its activity returns when it is warmed to 37 °C. Which explanation is correct?
options: At 5 °C, the enzyme is used up, and warming makes new enzyme molecules
At 5 °C, molecules collide less often, but the enzyme is not denatured
At 5 °C, the enzyme is denatured, and warming rebuilds the active site
At 5 °C, the substrate is denatured, so it cannot fit the active site
questions.explanation: Low temperature slows molecular movement, so fewer enzyme-substrate collisions occur, but the enzyme's shape is not permanently changed. Activity returns on warming. Denaturation by heat is usually irreversible.

questions.stem: Pepsin works in the stomach and trypsin in the small intestine. Which pair of optimum pH values is most likely?
options: Pepsin pH 7; trypsin pH 7
Pepsin pH 12; trypsin pH 5
Pepsin pH 2; trypsin pH 8
Pepsin pH 8; trypsin pH 2
questions.explanation: Each enzyme works best at the pH of its environment. The stomach is strongly acidic, so pepsin's optimum is about pH 2. The small intestine is slightly alkaline, so trypsin's optimum is about pH 8. Far from the optimum, the active site's shape changes.

questions.stem: In an experiment, the rate of an enzyme reaction rises as substrate concentration increases, then levels off. Adding more substrate at the plateau has no effect. What would raise the plateau?
options: Adding more enzyme, as all active sites are already occupied
Adding more substrate, as more collisions would then occur
Lowering the temperature, so fewer enzymes are denatured
Adding a competitive inhibitor, to keep the active sites free
questions.explanation: At the plateau every active site is occupied at any moment (the enzyme is saturated), so enzyme concentration limits the rate. More enzyme provides more active sites. More substrate cannot help when no free active sites remain.

questions.stem: A competitive inhibitor slows an enzyme reaction, but its effect becomes smaller as substrate concentration is increased. Why?
options: It binds away from the active site, so more substrate changes the enzyme's shape back
It denatures the enzyme, so more substrate is needed to rebuild the active site
It reacts with the substrate, so extra substrate leaves some unreacted molecules
It competes with the substrate for the active site, so more substrate outcompetes it
questions.explanation: A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and occupies the active site. At high substrate concentration, substrate molecules win most of the collisions, so the inhibition is reduced. A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the active site's shape, so extra substrate cannot overcome it.

questions.stem: A non-competitive inhibitor binds to an enzyme at a site away from the active site. What is its effect?
options: It changes the active site's shape, and adding substrate cannot overcome it
It blocks the active site directly, and adding substrate can overcome it
It raises the activation energy of the reaction by adding heat to the cell
It speeds up the reaction by holding the active site permanently open
questions.explanation: Binding at another (allosteric) site alters the enzyme's shape, so the active site no longer fits the substrate well. Because the inhibitor is not competing for the active site, extra substrate does not reverse the effect.

questions.stem: Starch and amylase were mixed at different temperatures, and the time for the starch to disappear was recorded: 20 °C, 8 min; 30 °C, 4 min; 40 °C, 2 min; 50 °C, 5 min; 60 °C, no change after 20 min. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The optimum temperature lies between 30 °C and 50 °C, and the enzyme is denatured by 60 °C
The optimum temperature is exactly 40 °C, and the enzyme is denatured at 50 °C
The rate falls steadily as temperature rises, because starch breaks down by itself
The enzyme works fastest at 60 °C, because the starch was digested before timing began
questions.explanation: The shortest time, and so the fastest rate, was at 40 °C, but with 10 °C steps the true optimum could lie anywhere between 30 °C and 50 °C. The reaction still occurred at 50 °C, so the enzyme was not fully denatured there. No digestion at 60 °C fits denaturation.

questions.stem: Phenylketonuria is an inherited metabolic disease in which an enzyme that converts the amino acid phenylalanine is not functional. How is it managed after newborn screening?
options: A diet low in phenylalanine, so that it does not build up in the body
A diet high in phenylalanine, to make up for the missing product
Injections of extra phenylalanine, so the faulty enzyme is saturated
Removing the enzyme's gene, so that phenylalanine is no longer made
questions.explanation: Without the functioning enzyme, phenylalanine accumulates and can harm brain development. Limiting phenylalanine in the diet prevents the build-up. Understanding which enzyme is faulty in a metabolic disease guides both its diagnosis and treatment.
